records.text: The above-entitled matter came on for oral argument before the Supreme Court of the United States at 11:05 a.m.

MR. MITCHELL: Justice Stevens, and may it please the Court: The Court has directed us to address, in addition to the question raised in the petition for writ of certiorari, the following question. Was petitioner's Federal constitutional claim properly raised before the Mississippi Supreme Court for purposes of 28 United States Code, section 1257?

MR. MITCHELL: Goodin is the case that the State cited for that purpose, but an analysis of what the Mississippi Supreme Court actually said at page 656 of the Southern Reporter, 787, is this. The Goodin jury did not face the dilemma of the Beck jury. Here, the jury's alternatives in the guilt phase were to convict Goodin of capital murder, simple murder, or to acquit him, which is the very purpose that the later cases -- and Beck itself explains.

JUSTICE SCALIA: Mr. Mitchell, my -- my problem is even more fundamental than Justice Souter's. Conceding that the rule in Mississippi is exactly the same as the Federal rule in Beck, it doesn't seem to me that arguing Mississippi law, just because it happens to be the same as Federal law, amounts to raising a Federal question.

MR. MITCHELL: It always has to comply with the -- with the Federal requirement, but as Justice Souter pointed out, it may be broader, for example, in situations where there might be a right to a -- a jury instruction on a lesser-related offense.
JUSTICE SOUTER: Is -- is that the case here too? One of the things that's neither here nor there I

MR. MITCHELL: We would respectfully submit that -- that even the Mississippi court has addressed that situation in -- in a case cited in -- in the briefs in Mease. And there, the defendant asked five times for instructions, lesser-included offense instructions, and never actually got them right.
JUSTICE GINSBURG: But then what would be a lesser-included offense? Because if it's not simple murder and it's not manslaughter, you haven't suggested a third that it might be.
JUSTICE SCALIA: I don't get your point. It doesn't have to be a -- a lesser-included offense --

JUSTICE SOUTER: Under Mississippi law, would he be entitled to a lesser offense instruction if he asked for the wrong lesser offense? I.e., in this case, if he failed to ask for heat of passion, would he still be entitled to a correct lesser instruction, even when he didn't ask for it?
Evidence shows that he was sprayed with mace, and at that point, he pulls out a gun and shoots.
JUSTICE SOUTER: May -- may I ask you? unclear on -- on lesser-included in Mississippi.

JUSTICE SCALIA: I think you confuse us by saying that. If you just left that out of your statement, felony murder is killing in the course of a crime. Don't say anything about intent. Intent is not an element of felony murder. Right?
